NEW YORK (CNN) -- New York's iconic Plaza Hotel will lose a figure nearly as synonymous with it as Eloise when its longest-serving doorman retires Thursday after 46 years on the job. Ed Trinka, whose retirement coincides with his 65th birthday, joined the hotel 1963. Ed Trinka, whose retirement coincides with his 65th birthday, joined the hotel's staff in 1963 as a teenager. He spent 40 years at the fabled lodging's Fifth Avenue entrance, relocating to its doorway facing Central Park South during the property's renovation and partial conversion to condominiums several years ago. Now as much a Central Park South fixture as the horse-drawn carriages that line the park's southern perimeter, the gregarious Trinka is known as the "mayor of 59th Street." On a recent afternoon, he seemed to know every other passerby, exchanging a constant stream of hellos with chauffeurs and doormen from adjacent tony apartment buildings and, of course, the Plaza's residents. Over his more than four decades manning the Plaza's entrance, Trinka has met countless celebrities -- or "all of them," as he puts it. After his first celebrity encounter at the hotel with the Beatles, he's catered to a long procession of big names, including Joe DiMaggio, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Liza Minnelli. Marla Maples, ex-wife of one-time Plaza owner Donald Trump, would regularly peck Trinka on the cheek when she saw him. Trinka says he has an autographed photo of Richard Nixon -- a token of gratitude from the former president -- hanging on proud display at his home. Trinka says he has thoroughly enjoyed his lengthy stay at the portal to history and glamour. "I never had a bad day in all the years." Nonetheless, with all those years at the hotel under his belt, Trinka felt it was time to "bow out gracefully." As he transitions to retirement, Trinka says he'll miss the front-row view of Central Park and the hotel's clientele -- the "greatest people in the world." He also concedes he'll miss "the women." The building's inhabitants are not eager for his departure. "He's a gentleman, refined -- you don't find these people anymore," lamented resident Joan Spain. Trinka's replacement, Jimmy O'Connell, is keenly aware of the large shoes he'll have to fill, saying he'd be satisfied if he "could be half the doorman" Trinka is. The hotel will bid farewell to Trinka in characteristically grand fashion on Thursday afternoon. After a champagne send-off in the hotel's landmarked Oak Room, its management will present him with an opportunity to view the Plaza from the vantage point of the countless guests he's greeted over the years: He'll be given a free stay at the hotel. In addition to a trove of anecdotes about celebrities, Trinka acquired something else during his tenure at the Plaza: a new name. Years ago, the hotel gave him a nametag that mistakenly read Edward, even though his full name is Edwin. He came to embrace the errant nametag, neglecting to correct people when they called him Edward and even naming his own son Edward.

NEW YORK (CNN) — After 46 years of service, the Plaza Hotel’s longest-tenured doorman will retire Thursday, ending a career that has made him almost as closely identified with the New York landmark as Eloise.

Ed Trinka, who turns 65 on the day of his retirement, began working at the hotel as a teenager in 1963. For four decades, he greeted visitors at the celebrated property’s Fifth Avenue doors. Several years ago, when the Plaza underwent renovations and was partly converted into condominiums, he moved to the entrance on Central Park South.

Trinka has since become as familiar a presence along Central Park’s southern edge as the horse-drawn carriages parked nearby. The outgoing doorman, nicknamed the “mayor of 59th Street,” appears to know nearly everyone in the area. On a recent afternoon, he continually traded greetings with drivers, doormen from neighboring upscale apartment buildings and Plaza residents.

During his more than four decades at the hotel’s entrance, Trinka says he encountered virtually every celebrity imaginable. His first famous guests were the Beatles, followed over the years by such notable figures as Joe DiMaggio, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Liza Minnelli.

Marla Maples, the former wife of onetime Plaza owner Donald Trump, often kissed Trinka on the cheek when they met. Former President Richard Nixon also gave him a signed photograph as a gesture of thanks, and Trinka proudly displays it at home.

Looking back, Trinka says he loved his long career at the threshold of a place associated with history and glamour.

“I never had a bad day in all the years,” he said.

Even so, after so much time at the Plaza, he decided the moment had arrived to “bow out gracefully.” In retirement, he expects to miss his close-up view of Central Park and the hotel’s guests and residents, whom he calls the “greatest people in the world.” He admits that he will also miss “the women.”

Those who live at the Plaza are sorry to see him leave.

“He’s a gentleman, refined — you don’t find these people anymore,” resident Joan Spain said.

Jimmy O’Connell, who will succeed Trinka, understands the scale of the role he is taking on. He said he would be pleased if he “could be half the doorman” Trinka has been.

The Plaza plans to honor him Thursday afternoon with a farewell befitting the hotel’s reputation. Following a champagne celebration in the landmarked Oak Room, management will allow Trinka to experience the hotel as the many guests he welcomed did: He will receive a complimentary stay.

Besides accumulating countless celebrity stories during his career, Trinka also picked up another first name. Many years ago, the hotel accidentally issued him a badge reading “Edward,” although his full name is Edwin. Rather than correcting the error, he eventually accepted the name, allowed people to call him Edward and even gave that name to his son.

## The “Mayor of 59th Street” Says Goodbye to the Plaza

For decades, he stood beneath the Plaza Hotel’s green-and-gold awning, opening car doors, hailing taxis and welcoming everyone—from first-time tourists to royalty—with the same polished warmth.

The veteran doorman became such a fixture at the corner of Fifth Avenue and Central Park South that colleagues and regular guests called him the “mayor of 59th Street.” He seemed to know everyone, and everyone seemed to know him.

His post offered a front-row seat to New York celebrity. Over the years, he greeted movie stars, musicians, presidents and visiting dignitaries. He remembered encounters with figures including Frank Sinatra, Liza Minnelli, Michael Jackson and Paul McCartney, although the stories he treasured most were not necessarily about the famous.

They were about children returning as adults, newlyweds coming back for anniversaries and families who made the Plaza part of their New York traditions. Guests who had met him once often discovered, years later, that he still remembered them.

That, he said, was the heart of the job: making people feel they belonged, even if they were only stepping through the revolving doors for a few moments.

The work was not always glamorous. It meant long hours on his feet through summer heat, winter winds and the constant churn of Midtown traffic. It required patience, discretion and an ability to stay composed amid crowds, cameras and impatient drivers. But he took pride in the uniform and in being the first and last face many guests saw.

His retirement was marked with a farewell celebration befitting a man who had spent so much of his life celebrating other people’s arrivals. Hotel employees, family members, friends and longtime guests gathered to applaud him, share memories and pose for photographs. There were hugs, speeches and more than a few tears.

For once, the doorman accustomed to holding the door for everyone else was the guest of honor.

As he prepared to leave his familiar corner, he reflected less on the stars he had met than on the relationships formed one greeting at a time. The Plaza would remain, as grand and busy as ever. Cars would continue to pull up, luggage would roll across the pavement and new doormen would take their places beneath the awning.

But 59th Street would be losing its mayor—and the Plaza, one of its warmest welcomes.

# After a lifetime opening doors at New York’s Plaza Hotel, its longest-serving doorman prepares to retire

**For decades, Edward welcomed celebrities, tourists and generations of returning guests. The name, like the career, began almost by accident.**

NEW YORK — Beneath the green awning of the Plaza Hotel, Edward became as much a fixture as the white-gloved service, gilded lobby and horse-drawn carriages waiting along Central Park South.

As the landmark hotel’s longest-serving doorman prepares to retire, he looks back not on the cold mornings, heavy luggage or endless New York traffic, but on the people who passed through the revolving doors.

“I never had a bad day in all the years,” he said.

It is the kind of statement that sounds almost impossible after a career spent outdoors in Manhattan’s heat, rain and snow. But Edward said the job gave him something new each day: familiar faces, first-time visitors and the chance to play a small role in moments guests would remember for years.

He greeted movie stars and business leaders, newlyweds and families arriving for their first glimpse of the famous hotel. Some guests returned year after year and asked for him by name.

That name, however, was never supposed to be his.

When he began working at the Plaza, he was handed a nametag that incorrectly read “Edward.” Rather than replace it, he put it on and went to work. Guests and colleagues started calling him Edward, and the mistake soon became permanent.

The nametag had effectively renamed him.

Over the years, Edward learned that being a doorman involved far more than opening car doors. He offered directions, found taxis, remembered returning guests and helped set the tone for an institution built on ceremony and personal service.

The Plaza changed around him. Ownership shifted, renovations reshaped parts of the building and New York itself evolved. Yet Edward remained at the entrance, offering the same welcome to each arrival.

Retirement will take him away from the daily rhythm of Central Park South, but not from the memories he made there. His legacy is measured less in years than in thousands of brief encounters — a greeting, a smile, a suitcase lifted or a door held open at just the right moment.

For generations of guests, Edward was not simply standing outside the Plaza. He was the Plaza.

And it all began with the wrong nametag.
